title: Osteoarthritis: Function First, Imaging Second
bottomLine: Typical osteoarthritis is a clinical diagnosis based on mechanical pain and function. Routine MRI is not needed, and treatment should emphasize exercise, strength, weight-related goals when relevant and topical or oral analgesic options matched to risk.
recognize: Pain worsens with use, morning stiffness is usually brief, and crepitus or bony enlargement may occur.
differentiate: Inflammatory arthritis has prolonged stiffness, synovitis and systemic features; septic arthritis is acutely hot and systemically concerning.
assessment: Assess affected joints, function, gait, falls, occupational demands, weight-related goals and analgesic risks.
workup: Plain radiographs are used when diagnosis is uncertain, severe, or surgery is being considered; MRI is not routine for uncomplicated OA.
management: Use therapeutic exercise, activity modification and topical NSAIDs where appropriate; oral NSAIDs require GI, renal and cardiovascular risk review; injections or surgery are selected for refractory disease.
medicationSafety: Avoid chronic opioid therapy for routine OA; systemic NSAIDs can worsen CKD, hypertension, heart failure and GI bleeding risk.
counselling: Explain that movement and strengthening are treatment, not evidence of joint damage.
followUp: Track function and pain rather than ordering repeated imaging.
examTrap: Ordering knee MRI for classic osteoarthritis before trying evidence-based conservative care.
oneLinePearl: OA treatment targets function; the x-ray does not need to look better for the patient to improve.

title: Gout: Crystal Arthritis With a Treat-to-Target Plan
bottomLine: Acute gout is intensely inflammatory monoarthritis, but first presentations—especially with fever—must not be assumed to be gout without considering septic arthritis. Long-term urate lowering is a separate decision from treating the flare.
recognize: Podagra is classic; CKD, diuretics, alcohol and metabolic disease increase risk.
differentiate: Septic arthritis can coexist with crystals; the presence of urate crystals does not absolutely exclude infection.
assessment: Assess fever, immune status, joint pattern, medications, CKD, prior flares, tophi and diet/alcohol context.
workup: Arthrocentesis is important when diagnosis is uncertain or infection is possible; serum urate can be normal during a flare.
management: Treat flare with NSAID, colchicine or corticosteroid selected for comorbidity; use urate-lowering therapy for appropriate recurrent, tophaceous or high-risk disease and titrate to target.
medicationSafety: Colchicine requires renal and interaction review; allopurinol is generally continued during a flare if already prescribed.
counselling: Do not frame gout as simply a dietary failure; medication often drives durable urate control.
followUp: Monitor serum urate and adherence during titration.
examTrap: Stopping chronic allopurinol during an acute flare.
oneLinePearl: Treat the flare and the urate as two related but distinct jobs.

title: Septic Arthritis: Aspirate Before the Joint Is Destroyed
bottomLine: An acutely hot, swollen, very painful joint with restricted passive range of motion is septic arthritis until excluded. Joint aspiration and prompt antibiotics are time-critical because cartilage destruction and sepsis can progress rapidly.
recognize: Risk rises with prosthetic joint, older age, immune suppression, bacteremia, injection drug use and recent joint procedure.
differentiate: Gout and pseudogout can look identical clinically; crystals do not rule out concomitant infection.
assessment: Assess fever, hemodynamics, joint prosthesis, skin infection, STI risk, bacteremia source and immune status.
workup: Obtain synovial cell count, Gram stain and culture with crystal analysis; blood cultures when systemically ill.
management: Drain the joint and start empiric antimicrobials after cultures when feasible without dangerous delay; involve orthopedics for prosthetic or difficult joints.
medicationSafety: Do not inject corticosteroid into a joint until infection has been reasonably excluded.
counselling: Explain urgency and possible need for operative washout.
followUp: Ensure culture-directed therapy and functional rehabilitation.
examTrap: Treating a hot swollen joint as gout solely because uric acid is high.
oneLinePearl: One hot joint plus fever deserves fluid, not assumption.
sourceBasis: Canadian infectious disease and rheumatology practice principles

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis: Early DMARD, Not Chronic Steroid Dependence
bottomLine: Persistent symmetric inflammatory small-joint synovitis with prolonged morning stiffness should trigger early rheumatology referral. Disease-modifying therapy should begin early; corticosteroids are not the long-term disease-control strategy.
recognize: MCP, PIP and wrist synovitis, prolonged morning stiffness and functional decline are typical.
differentiate: OA favours DIP/bony change and brief stiffness; viral arthritis and psoriatic disease may mimic RA.
assessment: Document swollen/tender joints, extra-articular disease, smoking, pregnancy plans, infection and vaccination status.
workup: RF and anti-CCP support but do not replace clinical diagnosis; obtain inflammatory markers and baseline labs/imaging appropriate to DMARD planning.
management: Refer early and use treat-to-target DMARD therapy according to current CRA living guidance; optimize vaccination, smoking cessation and cardiovascular risk.
medicationSafety: Methotrexate is teratogenic and requires blood/liver monitoring; biologic and targeted agents require infection screening and therapy-specific surveillance.
counselling: Explain that controlling inflammation prevents structural damage even when pain is temporarily manageable.
followUp: Disease activity and drug toxicity should be reassessed regularly.
examTrap: Using repeated steroid bursts for months while delaying DMARD referral.
oneLinePearl: RA joint damage is prevented by early disease modification, not by repeated symptom suppression.
sourceBasis: Canadian Rheumatology Association living RA guideline, updated 2026

title: Systemic Lupus: Symptoms Become Dangerous When Organs Are Involved
bottomLine: SLE is a clinical-serologic systemic disease. New proteinuria, hematuria, neurologic disease, thrombosis, cytopenias, myocarditis or pulmonary disease changes the urgency and usually requires specialty escalation.
recognize: Photosensitive rash, inflammatory arthritis, oral ulcers, Raynaud phenomenon and cytopenias are common features.
differentiate: A positive ANA is sensitive but nonspecific and is not a diagnosis by itself.
assessment: Assess renal, neurologic, cardiopulmonary, hematologic and obstetric symptoms; review medications and infection risk.
workup: Use urinalysis/protein quantification, CBC, renal function, complements and disease-specific antibodies guided by the clinical syndrome.
management: Hydroxychloroquine is foundational for many patients; organ-threatening disease requires rheumatology/nephrology-directed immunosuppression.
medicationSafety: Hydroxychloroquine requires retinal surveillance; immunosuppression requires infection and pregnancy planning.
counselling: Discuss sun protection, pregnancy planning and cardiovascular risk.
followUp: Trend organ-specific disease activity rather than ANA titre.
examTrap: Repeating ANA to monitor lupus activity.
oneLinePearl: ANA helps open the lupus question; organ findings determine the danger.

title: PMR and Giant Cell Arteritis: Vision Is the Emergency
bottomLine: New headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication or visual symptoms in an older adult with inflammatory symptoms can signal giant cell arteritis. If vision is threatened, start corticosteroid treatment immediately and do not wait for biopsy or imaging.
recognize: PMR causes bilateral shoulder or hip girdle pain and prolonged stiffness; GCA can coexist.
differentiate: Tension headache and migraine do not typically produce jaw claudication or ischemic visual symptoms in this age group.
assessment: Ask visual symptoms, jaw/tongue claudication, constitutional symptoms, limb claudication and PMR symptoms; check temporal arteries and full neurologic/eye status.
workup: ESR/CRP and CBC support inflammation; temporal artery ultrasound/biopsy and vascular imaging follow the local pathway.
management: Treat suspected GCA promptly with high-dose corticosteroids, using emergency ophthalmology/rheumatology pathways for visual symptoms; PMR uses lower steroid doses with monitoring.
medicationSafety: Long-term corticosteroids require bone, glucose, blood-pressure and infection-risk management.
counselling: Teach patients to report new visual symptoms immediately.
followUp: Monitor inflammatory symptoms, steroid toxicity and large-vessel complications.
examTrap: Waiting for a temporal artery biopsy before treating a patient with suspected GCA and acute visual symptoms.
oneLinePearl: GCA treatment protects vision; tissue confirmation comes after protection starts.

title: Axial Spondyloarthritis: Inflammatory Back Pain Is Not Mechanical Back Pain
bottomLine: Back pain beginning young, improving with exercise, worsening with rest and accompanied by prolonged morning stiffness or extra-articular inflammation should raise axial spondyloarthritis. Normal plain radiographs do not exclude early disease.
recognize: Uveitis, psoriasis, IBD and enthesitis are important associations.
differentiate: Mechanical pain is often activity-related and improves with rest; inflammatory pain behaves differently.
assessment: Ask onset age, nocturnal pain, morning stiffness, response to exercise, uveitis, psoriasis, IBD and family history.
workup: Use inflammatory markers, HLA-B27 selectively and sacroiliac imaging according to probability and rheumatology pathway.
management: Exercise/physiotherapy and NSAIDs are first-line for many patients; persistent active disease may require biologic/targeted therapy under current CRA/SPARCC living guidance.
medicationSafety: Biologic/targeted therapies require infection screening and vaccination planning.
counselling: Encourage movement and smoking cessation; discuss eye emergency symptoms.
followUp: Track function, spinal mobility and extra-articular disease.
examTrap: Ruling out axial spondyloarthritis because the lumbar x-ray is normal.
oneLinePearl: Inflammatory back pain improves with movement; early disease may be radiographically silent.
sourceBasis: CRA/SPARCC Living Guideline for Axial Spondyloarthritis, updated 2026

title: Psoriatic Arthritis: Look Beyond the Skin Plaque
bottomLine: Psoriatic arthritis can involve peripheral joints, spine, entheses and dactylitis, sometimes before obvious psoriasis is recognized. Early rheumatology referral prevents structural damage.
recognize: Dactylitis, nail pitting, DIP arthritis and enthesitis are characteristic clues.
differentiate: RA is typically symmetric small-joint synovitis without classic dactylitis/nail psoriasis; gout may mimic acute monoarthritis.
assessment: Inspect scalp, umbilicus, gluteal cleft and nails; ask family psoriasis, inflammatory back pain and eye/IBD symptoms.
workup: Diagnosis is clinical supported by inflammatory labs and imaging; RF/anti-CCP may help distinguish overlap but do not define PsA.
management: Use early rheumatology-directed DMARD/biologic therapy matched to domains; coordinate dermatologic treatment.
medicationSafety: Some systemic treatments affect liver, infection risk and pregnancy.
counselling: Explain that skin severity does not predict joint severity.
followUp: Track joint, enthesis, skin and functional outcomes.
examTrap: Assuming mild psoriasis cannot be associated with severe inflammatory arthritis.
oneLinePearl: Psoriasis can be quiet while psoriatic arthritis is loud.

title: Fibromyalgia: Central Pain Without Inventing Inflammation
bottomLine: Fibromyalgia is widespread nociplastic pain with fatigue, sleep and cognitive symptoms. It is diagnosed clinically after targeted exclusion of important mimics; repeated inflammatory panels and opioids usually cause more harm than benefit.
recognize: Widespread pain, nonrestorative sleep, fatigue and sensory sensitivity are typical.
differentiate: Inflammatory arthritis produces objective synovitis; myopathy produces weakness rather than pain alone; hypothyroidism and sleep apnea can mimic fatigue.
assessment: Assess sleep, mood, trauma history, function, physical activity, medications and objective inflammatory or neurologic signs.
workup: Use limited targeted tests for plausible mimics rather than extensive autoimmune screening in the absence of signs.
management: Use education, graded physical activity, sleep optimization, psychological strategies and selected neuromodulating medication.
medicationSafety: Avoid chronic opioids; sedating polypharmacy can worsen fatigue and function.
counselling: Validate symptoms without falsely labelling tissue inflammation or damage.
followUp: Measure function, sleep and participation rather than pain score alone.
examTrap: Ordering ANA/RF repeatedly because the patient has widespread pain without objective inflammatory findings.
oneLinePearl: Fibromyalgia is real pain without an inflammatory-joint treatment target.

title: Shoulder Pain: Rotator Cuff, Frozen Shoulder, or Referred?
bottomLine: Shoulder diagnosis starts with active versus passive range of motion, strength and referred-pain screening. Routine MRI is not the first step for most atraumatic shoulder pain.
recognize: Rotator cuff disease causes painful arc or weakness; adhesive capsulitis restricts both active and passive motion.
differentiate: Cervical radiculopathy, cardiac ischemia and diaphragmatic pathology can refer pain to the shoulder.
assessment: Assess trauma, weakness, ROM, neck symptoms, systemic/cardiac red flags and functional demands.
workup: Use x-ray for trauma, arthritis or chronic structural concern; ultrasound can assess cuff; MRI is reserved for specific surgical or complex indications.
management: Use activity modification, analgesia and physiotherapy; injections may help selected subacromial or adhesive-capsulitis cases.
medicationSafety: Steroid injection should not be repeated indiscriminately and must not be performed through infection.
counselling: Encourage guided movement rather than prolonged immobilization in most atraumatic conditions.
followUp: Persistent weakness or failure of conservative care may require imaging/referral.
examTrap: Ordering shoulder MRI before examining passive motion and strength.
oneLinePearl: Passive motion is the shortcut to separating frozen shoulder from many cuff problems.

title: Acute Knee Injury: Fracture, Ligament, Meniscus, or Extensor Failure?
bottomLine: Acute knee assessment should identify fracture and neurovascular or extensor-mechanism emergencies first, then use mechanism and examination to distinguish ligament and meniscal injury. MRI is not the initial test for every swollen knee.
recognize: Immediate hemarthrosis after pivot trauma suggests ACL/patellar dislocation or fracture; locking can suggest displaced meniscal injury.
differentiate: Septic arthritis and gout can mimic a traumatic swollen knee if the history is unclear.
assessment: Assess weight bearing, effusion, extensor mechanism, joint-line tenderness, ligament stability and distal neurovascular status.
workup: Use an Ottawa Knee Rule-type validated fracture rule where appropriate; x-ray for indicated fracture risk, MRI for persistent internal derangement when it will change management.
management: Protect significant injury, control pain/swelling and refer locked knee, extensor rupture, fracture or major instability; early rehabilitation is appropriate for many stable injuries.
medicationSafety: Avoid prolonged immobilization without indication because of stiffness and VTE risk.
followUp: Re-examine after acute swelling improves if internal injury remains unclear.
examTrap: Ordering MRI before x-ray in a patient who meets a validated fracture-imaging rule.
oneLinePearl: Acute knee care starts with fracture, extensor function and neurovascular status.

title: Low Back Pain: Red Flags, Function, and No Routine Imaging
bottomLine: Most acute low back pain is nonspecific and improves without imaging. Image urgently when neurologic compromise, infection, fracture, malignancy or major systemic disease is plausible; otherwise keep patients active and avoid bed rest.
recognize: Mechanical pain varies with movement and lacks systemic or progressive neurologic signs.
differentiate: Radiculopathy follows nerve-root symptoms; cauda equina, epidural abscess and malignant compression are emergencies.
assessment: Assess trauma, osteoporosis/steroids, fever, cancer, IV drug use, immune status, leg weakness, saddle sensation and bladder/bowel function.
workup: No routine imaging for uncomplicated acute nonspecific back pain; MRI for neurologic/infectious/malignant red flags.
management: Use reassurance, activity, heat/exercise and appropriate analgesia; avoid routine opioids and prolonged bed rest.
medicationSafety: NSAID, muscle-relaxant and opioid risks must be individualized.
counselling: Explain that early movement is safe in uncomplicated back pain.
followUp: Persistent or worsening symptoms require reassessment rather than automatic repeated imaging.
examTrap: Ordering lumbar MRI for uncomplicated two-day mechanical back pain with a normal neurologic exam.
oneLinePearl: No red flags means movement and time usually beat imaging.

title: Bone Pain: Fracture, Stress Injury, or Osteomyelitis?
bottomLine: Focal bone pain after trauma or repetitive load suggests fracture or stress injury; focal pain with fever, wound or bacteremia risk raises osteomyelitis. Normal early x-rays do not reliably exclude either stress fracture or osteomyelitis.
recognize: Diabetes foot ulcers, injection drug use, recent surgery and bacteremia increase osteomyelitis risk.
differentiate: Cellulitis involves soft tissue; septic arthritis localizes to the joint; malignant bone lesions can cause night pain/pathologic fracture.
assessment: Assess trauma/load, fever, skin ulcer/wound, neurovascular status, diabetes/neuropathy and systemic cancer/infection risk.
workup: Use x-ray initially for many fractures; MRI is more sensitive for occult stress injury and osteomyelitis; obtain cultures before prolonged antibiotics when feasible.
management: Immobilize and refer unstable/open fractures; osteomyelitis requires antimicrobial and often surgical/source-control planning.
medicationSafety: Do not give prolonged empiric antibiotics to chronic bone infection before obtaining meaningful cultures when the patient is stable.
counselling: Stress injuries need graded return and correction of bone-health or training factors.
followUp: Confirm healing or infection response with the appropriate specialty pathway.
examTrap: Ruling out osteomyelitis from a normal early plain x-ray.
oneLinePearl: Early bone infection can be radiographically quiet.
sourceBasis: Canadian orthopedic and infectious-disease practice resources
